title: Design the spread as a complete meal
focus: Start with the main dishes and build the sides, salads and sauces around them. More trays do not necessarily create a better buffet; a balanced selection makes it easier for guests to choose a satisfying plate. Consider where dietary options will sit and how they will be identified. For a larger room, discuss whether one serving line is sufficient or whether additional access points would help. The team and equipment should be sized for replenishment throughout the agreed period.

sections.title: Build a buffet guests can use comfortably
paragraphs: Start with a balanced meal rather than the largest possible dish count. Choose mains that work together, a substantial vegetarian option, complementary sides and a dessert selection. Explain the mix of adults and children, the meal time and whether guests will have already eaten canapés before the buffet opens.

The serving area needs space for queues, plates and replenishment. Tell us whether guests will arrive at once or eat in smaller groups, and whether there is room for more than one service point. The kitchen or preparation area should allow the team to replace dishes without carrying equipment through a crowded dining space.

Confirm serving equipment, dish labels, crockery, staffing and collection in the written quote. The team’s responsibilities during service and after the meal should be clear. If your venue has limited space, compare drop-off catering or passed canapés before deciding that a buffet is the best format.

sections.title: Give the menu a clear direction
paragraphs: Begin with a few dishes or flavours that your guests will enjoy, then build a balanced selection around them. A strong menu includes variety in texture, colour and richness without trying to cover every possible preference with a separate dish. The most useful question is how the food will work as a complete meal or reception.

Consider the time of day and the length of service. A short welcome reception needs a different amount and style of food from an evening where canapés replace dinner. Similarly, a working lunch should be easy to serve and enjoy within the available break.

Menu examples are a starting point for discussion. Ingredients, dietary variations and the practical requirements of your venue need to be reviewed before the final selection is confirmed. That gives the team room to recommend food that suits the occasion and can be served well.

sections.title: Plan quantities around the format, not just the headcount
paragraphs: Give separate adult and child numbers, explain whether the buffet replaces a full meal, and share how long guests will be eating. Canapés beforehand, a later meal or staggered arrivals all change the menu discussion; a headcount alone does not describe the service.

Choose a balanced selection of mains, vegetables, starches, salads and desserts rather than ordering every dish in equal quantities. Explain dietary requirements early and agree how alternatives will be identified and served. The final menu and quantities need to work together.

Ask who lays out the food, replenishes dishes, manages serving equipment and clears the buffet afterwards. If you intend to serve a delivery yourselves, compare that scope with a staffed buffet before deciding which quote fits your event.
